newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Ghana's Annan leads U.N. race but France blocks him.
newsitem.headline: Ghana's Annan leads U.N. race but France blocks him.

text.p: The contest for the post of U.N. secretary-general was deadlocked on Wednesday, with the head of U.N. peacekeeping operations, Kofi Annan of Ghana, leading the field of four African candidates but unable to shake off a potential French veto.

After two unofficial Security Council polls on Tuesday and another three on Wednesday, Annan remained the only candidate who consistently obtained more than the nine votes needed to win council endorsement once official balloting takes place.
Further balloting was set for Thursday but few expect a breakthrough immediately as France contemplates its next move.

On Wednesday his support hovered between 11 and 12 votes. But each time the votes against him included one cast by a permanent member of the 15-nation Council -- believed to be France. The other permanent members with veto power are the United States, Russia, Britain and China, who all voted for Annan, diplomats said.
The person formally nominated by the council once an official vote is held is certain to be endorsed by the 185-nation General Assembly.
Annan's nearest rival was Ivory Coast Foreign Minister Anara Essy, who presided over the General Assembly in 1994-95 and is thought to be France's favourite.

His support hovered between six and seven votes in Wednesday's balloting but he was opposed each time by two veto-bearing permanent council members -- widely thought to be the United States and Britain.

The other two candidates are Hamid Algabid of Niger, current secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, and Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah of Mauritania, a former foreign minister and U.N. envoy for Burundi.

Neither obtained more than four votes apiece on Wednesday, while their negative tallies included in each case the opposition of two permanent council members -- again believed to be the United States and Britain.
With Annan apparently the only viable candidate left in the race, diplomats said France was quietly sounding out opinions on other potential nominees from Africa.

They were Lakhdar Brahimi, an ex-Algerian foreign minister and head of the U.N. operation in Haiti, and Alassane Outtara, also of the Ivory Coast, a vice president at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and a former prime minister.

Africa has been given priority so far since it is an unwritten tradition for a secretary-general to be given two five-year terms. If Boutros-Ghali, an Egyptian, is denied a second term, council members have said that his successor should be an African.
If unofficial balloting proves this to be impossible, candidates from other continents might be accepted, with speculation that Asia should be given an opportunity.

In keeping with the secrecy surrounding the election of a secretary-general, council President Francesco Paolo Fulci of Italy gave reporters no details of the voting, saying only: "No conclusive result has yet been reached and therefore the straw poll goes on for the four names that you already know."

Still waiting in the wings is the incumbent secretary-general, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose five-year term expires Dec. 31. He was vetoed by the United States in formal balloting November 19 despite enjoying the backing of all 14 other council members.

Boutros-Ghali suspended his candidacy Dec. 4 and could reactivate it any time. But he is believed certain to be vetoed again by the United States, which insists the United Nations needs new leadership to carry out reforms.
